title.en: The Lonely Brothers and the Swift Kivigtok Bride
title.zh: 孤身兄弟與疾行的奇維托克新娘

region.en: Fiord of the west coast and the far side of the inland ice
region.zh: 西岸峽灣與內陸冰蓋彼端

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; abridged from one manuscript, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two housekeeping brothers steal a wife from a rocky point — a kivigtok, endowed with supernatural swiftness, who vanishes from between them and reappears mending their boots. Winning her confidence, they prosper until homesickness for her own brothers sends the whole family across the interior of Greenland; she leads at superhuman pace and is recognized by the little nephew who has never seen her. At the hook-and-crook feast the eldest visitor slowly pulls each host's arm to his breast, skinning it — then throws the giant champion a whole day's wrestle out among the spectators; the hosts' mysterious 'windlasses' prove to be walrus-teeth stuck in the ice for seal-hunting, and the brothers go home never to be seen again.
summary.zh: 操持家務的兩兄弟從巖角搶來一位妻子——疾行如飛的奇維托克人；她在他們之間憑空消失，又在家中補靴重現。贏得她的信任後家道興旺；她思親心切，竟領全家橫越格陵蘭內陸——她始終走在前面，令兩位獵手難以跟上。 hook-and-crook 摔跤宴上，長兄緩緩把每位主人的手臂拉到胸前、扯下臂皮；再與巨人冠軍摔足一整天，將其拋入觀眾之中。主人們的『絞盤』原來是插在冰上的海象牙獵具。歸途之後，兄弟們再也無人見過。

sensitivity.note: Kivigtok = those who fled from mankind to the desolate interior, believed to acquire supernatural swiftness and longevity (Rink's note). The cross-country journey is a transplanted motif per Rink.

passages.text: Two brothers had taken up their abode at a fiord, living alone, and having no female assistance were obliged to cook and make their garments themselves. One day out kayaking they passed a little rocky point, and turning their eyes landwards observed a woman standing on the beach. The eldest brother went ashore to fetch her, but when he approached she fled, at first slowly, till when he commenced to run she hurried on so that he gave her up and returned to his kayak. The younger brother ascended the beach, and as he approached she stood quiet, making no resistance, but let him take her down. They fastened the kayaks together with strings, and when she was seated behind the men she said to the eldest brother, 'I observed thy intention to be bad, so I fled; but thy brother there has a better disposition.' They paddled homewards keeping a sharp look-out upon her — but it happened they left off watching for a moment, and instantly they heard a clattering noise, and there she was gone; searching all around, no traces anywhere, they gave her up, saying, 'No matter, perhaps she was not a real woman' — that is, she had fled from mankind and was a Kivigtok, endowed with supernatural swiftness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They again untied their kayaks and made for home — but lo, there she was, standing outside the tent mending their boots. They ran up to her in case she wanted to run away, but she said to them, 'Pray let go your hold of me, I don't want to leave you.' For the first few days they were unwilling to leave her alone; afterwards they started but did not leave her neighbourhood, and did not venture away for any length of time until she had said, 'I like to stop with you, and ye may go as far as ye like.' Employing all their time in hunting, having a woman at home to cook and sew, they got more prosperous than before. She bore a male child in due time; but from that period her manners were altered, and she grew restrained and silent. Questioned at night, she answered: 'It is because of our baby boy; I would like him so much to go and see his mother's brothers. I cannot forget those dear ones, and that is the reason why I have grown so silent.' The brothers agreed they could not deny her the pleasure, and would accompany her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Delighted at the prospect, she packed up a bundle of boots and several new pairs of soles, and they started to cross the country; the wife with the child in the amowt constantly went ahead, and the others could scarcely keep up. For several days they wandered on until she exclaimed, 'If my brothers be still alive, and are to be found in the old place, we shall certainly come in sight of their sea to-morrow; I recognise all the mountain-hills of my old home.' Towards evening they sighted an open water and all began crying for joy, obliged to stop a little; they lay down for the night and descended the hillside in the morning, where a great many tents appeared in the valley below. Pointing to one remarkable for its greater size, she cried, 'That is the tent belonging to my relatives, but I would fain go down by myself; meanwhile you must keep behind' — and so she went. An old woman came forth from a tent holding a child by one arm, carrying a large seal-skin for sole-leather in her other; all of a sudden the little one turned round, exclaiming, 'Why, is not that my aunt coming there?' — 'No, don't speak such foolish things. Thou knowest very well thy aunt fled away never to return any more, because of these quarrels and fights for her sake.' Still the boy went on, 'Indeed, indeed, it is my aunt, and there she is coming!' — she got into a passion and tore out the peg-holes in the skin; then for the first time she looked up and cried out, 'That is she, sure enough. Why did not I believe the little one?' and went on caressing the boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Each of the brothers cried out, 'Oh, my dear sister! ye have not cared so much for her as I have; ye have not missed her so much neither; ye have not longed so much for her as I have done' — and each wanted to be the first to greet her and take hold of her, out of reverence for the eldest allowing him to give her welcome first. The men waiting on the mountainside were brought down, the tent entrance soon blocked with inquisitive neighbours eager to see the travellers who had crossed the whole breadth of the country; for joy at the meeting the brothers could do nought but sit down together and regard each other lovingly. In the evening the eldest proposed amusements, and they agreed to try strength at hook-and-crook: a skin was drawn forth, 'When strangers meet, one always likes to see which is the better man,' and the host undressed and seated himself on it; one of his own brothers sat down opposite, they hooked arms, and the eldest of the two beat his brother's back vigorously to encourage him to pull hard — yet neither he nor any of the brothers were able to stretch out his arm. The eldest of the visitors whispered to his brother, 'I shall first take my chance, then thou take thine' — undressed, sat down, hooked his right arm inside his adversary's, and gathering all his strength, slowly pulled on the arm till it touched his own breast; the other tried to draw him back, his features growing quite convulsed, the skin coming off his arms in the attempt. They tried the left arms with the same result; and at last the host rose: 'I now see that we have acquired some very strong friends... We, too, have got a man of great strength among us, and ye will scarcely escape him; I almost fear you won't come off alive.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning a call was heard outside: 'The visitors are requested to come and fight!' — a number of people ascending the heights to a plain where a still greater crowd formed a circle about a fellow with a frame like a giant. 'It won't do for thee to go first — thou dost look so very dejected; I had better go myself' — and at sunrise the elder brother suddenly rushed at the champion, taking him by surprise. At sunset they were still fighting; 'I must try to throw him over before I get too tired' — taking hold of him he slowly lifted him off his feet and held him swinging in the air; noticing a pole stuck up among some rocks, he did not choose to knock him down against that, but hurled him right out among the spectators, where he fell, the blood gushing from his mouth. A loud roar rose among the people — some rejoiced, others wept — and descending to the valley they all gathered around the eldest visitor merely to have the satisfaction of having touched him; some said, 'Thou shalt have my windlass in reward for that job,' which he did not understand at the time. The whole crowd vanished with one cry, 'Ye shall be our masters henceforth.' When frost set in, the visitors accompanied the men to see their ways of hunting: far beyond the shore they fell in with the frost-smoke and the first apertures in the ice, at the edge of which walrus-teeth had been stuck down — these were what they had been calling their windlasses. 'Do not try to harpoon the big ones, but aim at the little firth-seals, and leave the others to me' — each harpooned a small seal and wound his harpoon-string round one of the large walrus-teeth; when the seals were slaughtered and they prepared to return, letting the elder take the lead, he had not gone far before, turning round, he remarked, 'Now ye may go on just as ye like' — and went off as if carried by the wind. The others came home late; the brothers, forestalling them on another day with a large seal each, had the supper already before the master of the house on his entry: 'We fear the meat has got tough, and has lost its flavour; it is ever so long since we boiled it.' He was glad he had got such able and clever helpmates. When spring came on, the brothers began to long for their own home, and asked their former companion whether she preferred to stay or go with them — 'I will rather return with you.' Her parents making no objections, they went away together, and were never more seen or heard of by any of their kinsmen after the day of their departure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.

title.en: Sikutluk: The Killing Sorrow That Devoured Him
title.zh: 西庫特盧克：噬人的殺戮之痛

region.en: Inland glaciers and the erkilek coast
region.zh: 內陸冰川與厄基萊克海岸

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Persuaded to shoot his cousin's only dog, Sikutluk is trapped into a quarrel and shoots his beloved cousin dead — then stones the boat and tent and wanders off killing everything he meets: the she-amarok howling over her dead cubs ('Ah, my cousin, my beloved cousin, I murdered thee!'), the buck-carrying male, a kilivfak whose cave filled with its tumbling body. Fleeing across the glaciers, he and his wife fall in with men who are really erkileks; when he goes back for kinsmen and never returns, an angakok's clairvoyance names the male amarok as his devourer, and his wife lives on with the foreigners until her death.
summary.zh: 西庫特盧克被表兄設計射殺其唯一的狗，繼而在爭執中失手射死摯愛的表兄——用巨石封埋船與帳，攜妻遠走，見活物即殺：哀號於死崽之上的母狼（『唉，我的表兄，我的至愛表兄，是我害了你』）、銜鹿而歸的公狼、以及墜入洞穴的奇獸。穿越冰川後，他們投宿的『人們』其實是厄基萊克妖族；他返鄉尋親一去不返，巫師遙視斷言：是那頭公狼把他吞了。其妻遂與異族同住至終老。

sensitivity.note: Amarok (fabulous wolf), kilivfak (fabulous animal), erkilek (fabulous inlanders) per Rink's notes. Killing spree recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Sikutluk and his cousin were living together and loved each other dearly; at that settlement the cousin was the only one who possessed a dog. One day Sikutluk observed his cousin sitting before his tent doing some work, the dog beside him; when he came close up the cousin suddenly said, 'Pray, shoot my dog.' 'No, I won't, because we are friends.' But the cousin still persuaded him — 'Pray do it, nevertheless'; he brought his bow accordingly, but not yet satisfied, the cousin again inquired, 'But wilt thou not really get vexed when it is too late?' 'No, indeed, I shall not' — and the other killed the dog. The cousin, however, took offence for all that, and challenged his friend, saying he had a mind to kill him at once; but Sikutluk shot him right through the breast, and he fell down dead. Immediately after this Sikutluk went and covered his cousin's boat and tent all over with heavy stones, and left the place along with his wife; but the murder he had committed had made him thirst for blood, and he went on intending to kill whatever he met with — at first content with killing ptarmigan and reindeer, both bringing with them as many arrows as they were able to carry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After a while they fell in with an aviarok. They first discovered the young ones, but towards evening the mother arrived with a young buck in her mouth; from their retreat they noticed her dropping the burden on finding that her young ones were killed, then sniffing the air, following the scent of human beings, and with a fearful howl coming running on towards them at full speed. The woman screamed, 'I fear she will devour us!' but he made no other reply than, 'Ah, my cousin, my beloved cousin, I murdered thee!' — and crept forth from his ambush, aimed at the beast, and killed it on the spot. They hid themselves again, and soon afterwards saw the male return, also carrying a buck between his teeth; after the same words, 'Alas, my cousin, my beloved cousin!' he shot this one also. They still wandered on and on, and killed everything living they met with on their way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the woman caught sight of a kilivfak, which stood scratching the earth with its feet. When the husband had also seen it, he first went to look out for a hole in the earth close by, where he ordered his wife to go and hide, and remain quiet till he should let himself down to her; he stole down to encounter the animal, bending to the ground whenever it turned to look round, creeping on when it stood scratching the earth. At last he had got quite close, ventured a shot at it, hurried back, and let himself fall down to his wife — after him came the wild beast tumbling down into the cave, where it entirely filled up the opening; but after much toil they got out again. They continued roaming further away, crossing the glaciers with him carrying his wife across the crevasses; at length he again reached the sea, and at the same time observed a kayaker close by, who said he would take them to his own place if they would wait while he brought a boat — but the crew were all men. They took up with these people, but soon found out they had come among erkileks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Sikutluk told his wife that he would return and look for some of their kinsmen, naming a certain time by which they expected to be back; but in vain they waited for him. When the appointed time had elapsed, they promised an angakok a great reward if he could tell what had befallen the traveller. After some meditation he replied, 'I observed he killed a pair of amaroks with their brood.' The wife acknowledged it. 'And a female kilivfak besides?' 'Indeed he did so.' 'Then be assured the male beast devoured him.' But the wife of Sikutluk lived on with the foreigners until the time of her death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl Who Fled to the Inlanders

region.en: Inland lakes and stone-boat roads of the inlanders
region.zh: 內陸湖沼與內陸人的石舟之路

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from imperfect manuscripts, one of the oldest traditions, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Exiled for breaking her sister's precious reindeer-horn needle, a girl weeps on a stone until a tall inlander — exiled likewise for spoiling his brother's snare — takes her home over the hills, past his idiot sister's betrayal ('Ye haven't got a sister-in-law like mine, with beads and necklace — a real nice one'), through the stone-boat voyage with shut eyes, the dancing feats (reindeer, hare, and peeled-skin transformations, one dancer crushing a woman and child), the vermin-boots that grow her new inland flesh and swiftness, and the duck-trap triumph — until, their son dead, he returns to his own people and is seen no more.
summary.zh: 因折斷姐姐珍貴的鹿角針而被逐的少女，在石上啜泣——一位同樣因弄壞兄弟珍貴羅網而被逐的高大內陸人將她帶回家。白痴妹妹洩密（『你們可沒有我這樣的弟媳——戴著珠串項鍊的海濱美人』）、閉眼乘石舟、觀舞（化鹿、化兔、剝皮起舞，一名舞者竟踏斃一對母子）、以蟲豸之靴長新肉而得內陸人的敏捷、鴨籠滿載的勝利——直到兒子病亡，他返回族人之中，從此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as preserving relations between Eskimo and Indians, with hints of the latter's dancing and disguising customs. Crushing death at the dance recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There was once a young maiden who happened to break her elder sister's needle, made of reindeer-horn and very precious. The sister got dreadfully angry, although she lived in great prosperity, being well married — so angry that she told her sister she might as well take herself off, and henceforth keep away from the coast-people. The girl at once obeyed, and wandered about the country for many a day. One night, sitting down on a stone crying, she heard a voice beside her: 'Why dost thou cry thus?' — turning round she saw a very tall man, whom she recognised to be an inlander, standing beside her. 'For what art thou crying?' 'Because I broke my sister's needle, and she sent me away.' 'And I was sent away in the same manner because I spoiled my brother's precious snare.' Then he asked her to follow him, and they went away together to his house, where he made her a present of deer-skins, some for outer garments and some for inner clothes, and took her for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

passages.text: This inlander used to go and catch eider-ducks in a certain lake by wading out into the water and taking the birds by stealth. One day he proposed that she should accompany him on a visit to his relatives, telling her that when they came in sight of the house he would call out, 'Kung, kung-kuyo!' and they would know him at once. They went; as soon as from one of the hill-tops they could make out the house of his relatives in the valley, he made the sign, and they heard the children of the place calling out, 'Somebody is saying, Kung, kung,' and his mother appearing in the doorway repeating the same words. They descended and entered the house; he had a sister who was an idiot (considered a clairvoyant) and very talkative, and told her not to mention that a coast-woman had come among them, going to hide his wife in some remote corner of the broad ledge — but when his brothers came in they at once remarked, 'There is a smell of coast-people about the place!' and when the fool went outside she could not forbear saying to his neighbours, 'Ye haven't got a sister-in-law like mine, with beads and necklace — a real nice one — one of the coast-women!' After this the inquisitive people thronged about the window to get a peep at the stranger, some creeping up on the roof to make themselves a peep-hole, and in no time the house was quite full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Subsequently there was talk of a boat shortly expected, and one morning it was announced to be coming — inuarutligaks, fabulous dwarf inlanders or mountain-elves. On coming up from the beach they stopped outside the house and commenced singing to one another, then brought forth gifts of skins, and stayed a whole month, enjoying each other's company, feasting a great deal, and singing songs continually. At one of their banquets an inlander stood forth and, by way of entertaining the assembly, sang and danced: during the dance he transformed himself into a reindeer, at which trick the children of the inuarutligaks got dreadfully frightened, so that he again quickly changed himself into a man. Another took upon himself the shape of a hare, but the inlanders' children cried out aloud and he hastened to re-change himself; another pulled the skin from off his whole body till it only adhered to a small portion between his eyes, putting it all right again when the urchins cried. At last one of the inuarutligaks came forth to dance, and he danced in such a way that the whole house soon leaned over, all the inmates rolling down to one side with such force that one woman and a child were crushed to death. The entertainment now ended, and the next day the inuarutligaks departed, after having first invited their late hosts to visit them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a month's time they made preparations to start, and had a boat made of stone for the purpose. They agreed that the coast-woman might as well be of the party, but told her not to open her eyes during the voyage, the boat not moving on if she did so; she complied, but as soon as the crew could make out the sound of children's voices they permitted her to open them again, and she perceived a very little house, wondering how they should all get room in it — while she was looking at it, it seemed to grow bigger, the inuarutligaks knowing how to enlarge their houses by means of rubbing them. They went inside, bringing their bundles of skin, one for each person, and commenced feasting and merry-making. One of the inuarutligaks stepped forward, and after having performed a dance flung himself down on the ground transformed into an orsighiak-stone (a sort of white, glistering felspar); the inlanders tried to lift it, but being quite unable, he soon rose up in his proper shape. One of the inlanders now advanced, fell to the ground, and was transformed into a common stone; but the inuarutligaks managed to lift it, and flung it against the door, where it flew to pieces — in this manner the inlanders lost one of their people, and they left on the following day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the summer-time preparations were made for reindeer-hunting, and the coast-woman was to accompany them. She had two girls for her enemies because she married so early, and they were always molesting her and trying to make her ridiculous, saying she was not so smart and lightfooted on the march as the inlanders; one added, 'To-day I even pursued and overtook a young deer!' On hearing this, the old woman of the house produced a pair of boots which she filled with all kinds of vermin, ordering her to put them on and tightening them round her legs, the husband encouraging her — 'She must needs bear it in order to get agile and smart.' But presently she fell into a swoon, and the skin dropped off her feet and legs; when restored to her senses she perceived new flesh and new skin growing on them, and she had now become swift and nimble as the inlanders themselves. On their return from the reindeer-hunt she said she longed for her relatives and was desirous to go and see them; the next summer her husband accompanied her thither. Approaching the coast-side they hailed a kayaker and asked him to bring a boat to take them the remainder of the way; on getting into it the inlander was dreadfully afraid, falling down flat on his face at the bottom of the boat, where he remained till he landed close to their home. They stayed that winter at her parents, and once her father said, 'I wish I could have got another son-in-law instead of this one — one who knew how to trap eider-ducks' — the inlander had a habit of stopping in the house all day, but at these words he only asked a trap of him; one day he returned all covered with ducks. The other men of the place in the winter-time often used to ridicule him, and always wanted to persuade him to accompany them out on the ice for the viowpok-hunt (seal-hunt by watching the breathing-holes). In the summer he resolved to visit his countrymen, and on parting said to his wife, 'If I find our son in health, I will return with more companions.' He set off, and did not return till next spring, and then reported that their son had died. He told his wife it was now his intention to return to his own people; and when he left they never saw any more of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
